title: What are Record Patterns and pattern matching for `switch` (Java 21), and how do they enable exhaustive, type-safe deconstruction of sealed hierarchies (algebraic data types)?
shortTitle: What are Record Patterns and pattern matching for switch (Java 21), and how do they enable exhaustive, type-safe deconstruction of sealed hierarchies?

s1_definition.profdef: Record patterns, standardized in Java 21, let you match a record and bind its components in one step, for example `case TransferEvent(String from, String to, BigDecimal amount)`, and they nest so you can destructure records inside records. Pattern matching for `switch`, also standard in Java 21, lets a switch test the runtime type of a selector and bind a variable per case, including type patterns, record patterns, and guards with `when`. Combined with a sealed hierarchy, where the permitted subtypes are known, the compiler can verify the switch is exhaustive, so if every permitted case is handled you need no default, and if you add a new subtype the switch fails to compile until you handle it. This is how Java expresses algebraic data types with compile-time-checked, type-safe deconstruction.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has a fixed, official list of exactly the kinds of payment events that can occur: a transfer, a deposit, and a withdrawal, and nothing else is allowed (the sealed hierarchy). A pattern-matching switch is like a sorting clerk who looks at each incoming event, instantly recognizes which of the fixed kinds it is, and in the same motion opens it up and reads out its details (record pattern deconstruction). Because the list of kinds is official and closed, the supervisor can guarantee the clerk has a procedure for every kind, and the day someone invents a new kind of event, the clerk's rulebook refuses to be approved until a procedure for it is added.
s1_definition.oneliner: Record patterns deconstruct records in a case, pattern-matching switch binds by runtime type with guards, and over a sealed hierarchy the compiler enforces exhaustiveness so adding a case becomes a compile error you cannot miss.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Record patterns, standardized in Java 21, let you match a record and bind its components in one step, for example `case TransferEvent(String from, String to, BigDecimal amount)`, and they nest so you can destructure records inside records. Pattern matching for `switch`, also standard in Java 21, lets a switch test the runtime type of a selector and bind a variable per case, including type patterns, record patterns, and guards with `when`. Combined with a sealed hierarchy, where the permitted subtypes are known, the compiler can verify the switch is exhaustive, so if every permitted case is handled you need no default, and if you add a new subtype the switch fails to compile until you handle it. This is how Java expresses algebraic data types with compile-time-checked, type-safe deconstruction.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has a fixed, official list of exactly the kinds of payment events that can occur: a transfer, a deposit, and a withdrawal, and nothing else is allowed (the sealed hierarchy). A pattern-matching switch is like a sorting clerk who looks at each incoming event, instantly recognizes which of the fixed kinds it is, and in the same motion opens it up and reads out its details (record pattern deconstruction). Because the list of kinds is official and closed, the supervisor can guarantee the clerk has a procedure for every kind, and the day someone invents a new kind of event, the clerk's rulebook refuses to be approved until a procedure for it is added.

**One line to remember:** Record patterns deconstruct records in a case, pattern-matching switch binds by runtime type with guards, and over a sealed hierarchy the compiler enforces exhaustiveness so adding a case becomes a compile error you cannot miss.

sections.s2_technical:
A type pattern in a switch tests the selector's runtime type and binds a variable, for example `case TransferEvent t -> ...`, which replaces the old chain of instanceof and casts. A record pattern goes further and destructures the record's components into named bindings in the same case, for example `case TransferEvent(String from, String to, BigDecimal amount) -> ...`, so you immediately have from, to, and amount without calling accessors. Record patterns nest, so if a record holds another record you can write a pattern inside a pattern and pull out deep fields in one line, and you can use var in the binding to let the compiler infer the component type.

Guards refine a case with a boolean condition using the when keyword, for example `case TransferEvent(var f, var t, var amount) when amount.compareTo(LIMIT) > 0 -> flagLargeTransfer(...)`, so you branch not just on shape but on values. The switch can be an expression that yields a value, which forces every path to produce a result and makes the logic compact. Null handling is explicit: a switch with patterns throws on null unless you add a case null, which removes a common source of bugs.

The real power appears with sealed hierarchies. If you declare `sealed interface PaymentEvent permits TransferEvent, DepositEvent, WithdrawalEvent`, the compiler knows the complete set of subtypes. A switch over a PaymentEvent that has a case for each permitted subtype is provably exhaustive, so the compiler does not require a default clause, and more importantly, the day someone adds a fourth permitted subtype, every exhaustive switch that does not handle it fails to compile. This turns a whole class of runtime surprises into compile-time errors, which is the essence of algebraic data types: a closed set of shapes plus pattern matching that the compiler checks for completeness. A senior nuance: prefer exhaustive switches without a default over a sealed type, because a default would silently swallow a newly added subtype and defeat the exhaustiveness check; use records as the data shapes and the sealed interface as the sum type; and remember guards are considered when checking that a dominant case does not shadow a later one, so order and guards matter and the compiler enforces that a more general pattern cannot precede a more specific one.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India processes several kinds of payment events, and the old code was a long chain of instanceof checks and casts that was easy to get wrong and silently fell through when a new event type appeared. This is exactly what pattern-matching switch with record patterns solves — it tests the type and deconstructs the data in one readable case.

Problem 2 — When the bank adds a new kind of payment event, every place that handles events must be updated, and missing one causes a production bug. This is exactly what a sealed hierarchy plus an exhaustive switch solves — the compiler refuses to build until the new case is handled, turning a runtime risk into a compile error.

The demo declares a sealed PaymentEvent with record subtypes, processes events with an exhaustive pattern-matching switch using record patterns and a guard for large transfers, and shows that no default is needed. Classes and steps: `PaymentEvent` (sealed) with `TransferEvent`, `DepositEvent`, `WithdrawalEvent` records, `PaymentProcessor` (exhaustive switch), and `PatternDemo`.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build with Java 21 (record patterns + pattern matching for switch are standard)
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the pattern-matching demo
java -cp target/classes com.bank.patterns.PatternDemo

# PROOF of exhaustiveness: add a new permitted subtype, e.g.
#   record ReversalEvent(String txnId, BigDecimal amount) implements PaymentEvent { }
# and add it to the permits clause — PaymentProcessor.describe() will FAIL TO COMPILE
# ("the switch statement does not cover all possible input values") until you add its case.
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a normal transfer, a large transfer, a deposit, a withdrawal, and a null, processed one by one.

Step 1 — The normal TransferEvent from Rajesh to Priya for Rs.50,000 enters the switch. The guarded large-transfer case is tested first but its when condition is false because 50,000 is not over the limit, so the plain TransferEvent record pattern matches, binding from, to, and amount in one step, and the summary is a normal transfer description.

Step 2 — The large TransferEvent for Rs.500,000 enters the switch, the guarded case's when condition is true, so it matches the guarded case and the summary flags it for review, showing that matching is on both shape and value.

Step 3 — The DepositEvent and WithdrawalEvent each match their own record pattern, binding the account and amount directly, producing their respective summaries without any instanceof or cast.

Step 4 — The null is handled by the explicit case null rather than throwing, and crucially the switch has no default clause, because the compiler proved it covers every permitted subtype of the sealed PaymentEvent; adding a new subtype would break the compile until a case is added.

```
2026-10-26 16:10:01 [INFO] Processed: transfer Rs.50000 SAV2001->CUR3001
2026-10-26 16:10:01 [INFO] Processed: LARGE transfer Rs.500000 SAV2001->CUR3001 (flag for review)
2026-10-26 16:10:01 [INFO] Processed: deposit Rs.25000 into CUR3001
2026-10-26 16:10:01 [INFO] Processed: withdrawal Rs.10000 from SAV2001
2026-10-26 16:10:01 [INFO] Processed: ignored null event
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  PaymentEvent (sealed: Transfer | Deposit | Withdrawal)
    │
    ▼ switch (event)   — tests runtime type AND deconstructs in one step
    ├─ case null                                           → "ignored null event"
    ├─ case TransferEvent(from,to,amount) when amount>LARGE → "LARGE transfer ... flag"
    ├─ case TransferEvent(from,to,amount)                   → "transfer ..."
    ├─ case DepositEvent(account,amount)                   → "deposit ..."
    └─ case WithdrawalEvent(account,amount)                → "withdrawal ..."
       (NO default — compiler proves exhaustiveness over the sealed set)

  Add ReversalEvent to permits ──► describe() FAILS TO COMPILE until a case is added
    = runtime surprise turned into a compile-time error (algebraic data type)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Record Patterns + Sealed Switch ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Algebraic Data Type: sealed interface (sum) + records (product)│
  │    WHY: closed, exhaustively-checkable set of shapes           │
  │ Visitor-replacement: pattern switch instead of double dispatch │
  │    WHY: add behavior in one place, compiler-checked complete   │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ O: add a subtype → compiler forces every switch to handle it   │
  │ L: each record substitutes PaymentEvent wherever expected      │
  │ S: processor only classifies/describes; records carry data     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ <<sealed>> PaymentEvent       │ permits exactly 3
  └───────────────┬──────────────┘
      ┌───────────┼─────────────────┐
      ▼           ▼                 ▼
  TransferEvent DepositEvent  WithdrawalEvent   (records = product types)
  (from,to,amt) (account,amt) (account,amt)

  ── Matching Rules (as prose) ─────────────────────────────────
  type pattern   : case TransferEvent t      (bind, no deconstruct)
  record pattern : case TransferEvent(a,b,c) (bind + deconstruct)
  guard          : ... when amount > LARGE   (branch on value)
  null           : case null                 (explicit, else throws)
  exhaustive     : no default over sealed set → add subtype = compile error

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. process(event) → describe(event)
  2.   → switch tests type + deconstructs components
  3.   → guard checks amount vs LARGE
  4.   → yields summary string (switch expression)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Record patterns and pattern matching for switch, both standardized in Java 21, work together to let me classify and deconstruct data in one readable step. A type pattern in a switch tests the runtime type of the selector and binds a variable, replacing the old chain of instanceof and cast. A record pattern goes further and destructures a record's components into named bindings right in the case, so instead of matching a TransferEvent and then calling accessors, I write a case that names from, to, and amount directly, and these patterns nest so I can pull fields out of records inside records in a single line.

I refine a case with a guard using the when keyword, so I branch not only on the shape of the data but on its values, for example treating a transfer over a limit as a large transfer that needs review. The switch can be an expression that yields a value, which forces every branch to produce a result and keeps the logic compact, and null is handled explicitly with a case null instead of silently throwing.

The real power is when the selector is a sealed type. If I declare a sealed interface that permits exactly a transfer, a deposit, and a withdrawal, the compiler knows the complete set of subtypes, so a switch with a case for each is provably exhaustive and needs no default. The crucial payoff is that the day someone adds a fourth permitted subtype, every exhaustive switch that does not handle it fails to compile. That turns a whole class of runtime surprises into compile-time errors, and that combination of a closed set of shapes with completeness-checked pattern matching is exactly what algebraic data types are.

In my banking work at National Bank of India this replaced a long, fragile chain of instanceof checks for payment events. I modeled the events as records under a sealed PaymentEvent interface, and the processor used one exhaustive pattern-matching switch with record patterns and a guard for large transfers, with no default clause. When we added a new event type, the build broke in every consumer until we handled it, which caught what used to be production bugs at compile time. The senior point I always stress is to deliberately avoid a default clause over a sealed type, because a default would silently swallow a newly added subtype and defeat the whole exhaustiveness guarantee, and that I let the compiler enforce case ordering so a more general pattern can never shadow a more specific one.

keyPoints: sealed: restrict which classes can extend/implement
permits: explicit list of allowed subclasses
Subclass must be: final, sealed, or non-sealed
Enables exhaustive switch/pattern matching — compiler checks all cases
